reason: Under the Consolidated billing feature set heading the quote says you can't enable other AWS services to integrate across all accounts or use policies to restrict what users and roles in different accounts can do.
The quote says only the management account in an organization (and standalone accounts) has access to the cost allocation tags manager in the Billing console; the claim keeps the organization scope.
The quote states creating member accounts and inviting existing accounts can be done only from the management account, not from a delegated administrator account.

The quote says Organizations automatically creates an IAM role named OrganizationAccountAccessRole by default, a different name can be given, and no other users or roles are created; the scope is limited to accounts created through Organizations, matching the page note.
One quote says the rules for organizations 'by default (Credit sharing turned on)'; the other says accounts must have credit sharing activated to give or receive shared credits.
In the list of rules for credit sharing turned off, the quotes say credits are applied to only the receiving account and only the payer account can turn credit sharing off or on.
The two decision-guide sentences state both halves of the claim verbatim.
The four table rows under 'When would you use it? / Recommended service' map each use case to Organizations, Control Tower, AWS Config and Security Hub CSPM as claimed.

The quote says an organization instance of IAM Identity Center helps manage workforce access to AWS accounts and lets you assign permissions and provision them to multiple accounts from a central place.
The quote defines the effective policy as rules inherited from root and OUs plus those directly attached, and the final set of rules that apply to the account.
Read with the table header (SCP | RCP | Declarative), the row gives No | No | Yes for governing service-linked roles.
The three bullets state root, OU (direct or any child OU) and account attachment behavior exactly as claimed, and the page notes it does not apply to SCPs or RCPs, matching the scope.
The quotes say joining accounts automatically inherit the declarative policy and a detached policy rolls the attribute back to its previous state.

The table row gives 0 minimum and 10 maximum for root, per OU and per account; the note in the same section of the snapshot says inherited policies do not count and all policy limits are hard limits, matching the qualifiers.
The two quotes under the Root definition state a declarative policy at root includes the management account, while an authorization policy such as an SCP does not apply to it.
The quote states both the purpose (prevent noncompliant actions) and the two VPC examples verbatim.
The quotes say declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane and that authorization policies regulate access to APIs while declarative policies apply at the service level.
The quote states central declaration and enforcement across an organization and that the configuration is always maintained when the service adds new features or APIs.

The quotes give the reduced management-account usage and the 'some administrative permissions' plus Organizations read-only permissions; the snapshot's prerequisite list right after (service supports delegated admins, enable trusted access) matches the condition.

The row supports 40,000 characters, but the section calls these values 'default maximums' and says increases can be requested for some of them, so the qualifier adjustable=false is not stated by the source.
The user-guide quote describes invitation and acceptance without leaving the current organization; the What's New post dated Nov 19, 2025 says this removed the previous standalone requirement.
The quotes state disabling trusted access does not prevent permitted users and roles, blocking requires removing IAM permissions or SCPs, and SCPs apply only to member accounts.
The first quote gives EC2, VPC and EBS scope; the account status report quotes name all six attributes as attributes of EC2 policies.
The quotes and context state custom error messages (including a custom URL such as an internal wiki link) on policy-caused API failures and that CloudTrail can flag such failures.
Under Amazon EBS in Supported attributes, the Snapshot Block Public Access attribute has policy effect 'Controls if Amazon EBS snapshots are publicly accessible'.
Under Expiration times for handshakes (timeouts), the request to enable all features has a 90 days limit.
The FAQ says for both methods (invite or create) you can move the account to an OU and it automatically inherits the OU's policies.
The FAQ answer states an AWS account can be a member of only one OU at a time.
The FAQ answer to the OU-structure billing question says the bill will not reflect the structure defined in the organization.
In the answer on SCPs, RCPs and declarative policies together, the quote names Config detective rules for monitoring and proactive rules to prevent non-compliant CloudFormation resources.
In context the consolidated billing functionality gives a single-payer account for all accounts and automatic default tiered-pricing benefits.
The quote says cost allocation tags in individual accounts categorize costs and the allocation is visible in the consolidated bill.
The FAQ answers yes, says AWS does not collect all standalone information at creation, and lists contact information, a valid payment method and a support plan as what must be updated.
The quotes say a created account can be transferred through an invitation and, once accepted, inherits the new organization's billing, support plans and policies.
In the FAQ answer contrasting declarative policies with SCPs, the quote says declarative policies give a simpler way to define configuration and customizable error messages explaining failures.
The quote states both parts verbatim.
The quote says adding a control covered by existing SCPs to a declarative policy serves as an additional layer of protection.
The quote says enforced declarative policies prevent non-compliant actions and the configuration is maintained for new APIs and features and for added resources, principals and accounts.
The FAQ says to navigate in the console to the integrated service and enable the integration there.
The quote says all organization entities are globally accessible except organizations managed in China, similar to IAM; the context adds no Region is specified.
